strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper cleanly decomposes the gap between full-sequence video diffusion models and interactive world models into (1) causal generation and (2) action conditioning, and addresses each with a targeted mechanism.

The 'mixed weight transfer' scheme for adapting non-causal temporal convolutions is a sensible and novel engineering contribution, with the shift-weight-transfer baseline providing a direct contrast, and the ablation (Table 3) shows it matters.

Frame-level action injection combined with independent action dropout is a principled way to extend classifier-free guidance to autoregressive rollout, and the counterfactual action-conditioning visualization (Figure 11) is a compelling qualitative demonstration.

Evaluation spans two distinct domains (real-world robot manipulation with RT-1, and game simulation with CS:GO), with multiple appropriate transfer baselines built on the same base model, standard video prediction metrics, hyperparameter tables, and honest failure-case analysis in the appendix.

The downstream Real2Sim policy evaluation experiment goes beyond video quality metrics and demonstrates the world model is actually useful for sequential decision-making, tracking real-world policy success trends (Figure 4).
The paper is clearly written, with full training/sampling pseudocode (Algorithms 1-2) and extensive implementation details supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the autoregressive training scheme is adopted directly from Diffusion Forcing [8], and the action-dropout CFG extension is a fairly straightforward application of standard classifier-free guidance practice to a frame-level condition; the paper's contribution is mostly a well-executed combination of existing techniques rather than a new method.

The comparison with DIAMOND on CS:GO is potentially unfair: Vid2World is a 1.1B-parameter model pre-trained on internet-scale video and fine-tuned on the domain, whereas DIAMOND is a small model trained from scratch at 150x280 resolution; the claimed 81.8% FVD improvement largely reflects this scale asymmetry rather than the transfer method itself. A scale-matched baseline or discussion is missing.

Inconsistencies and oddities in the numbers: in Table 1, Vid2World-NAR's FID (5.921) and Vid2World's FID (5.985) are substantially worse than fine-tuning baselines (~3.0), yet the text claims superiority; the ablation Table 3 reports FID around 6.8-7.0, differing from Table 1 even for the same configuration. The resolution of the metric-computation procedure (downsampling/cropping) may confound cross-model comparisons.

No report of inference latency/throughput despite 'interactive world models' being the central claim; autoregressive rollout with 50 DDIM steps per frame is likely far from real-time, and the practical interactivity of the resulting model is not quantified.

The policy evaluation uses human evaluation as the verifier with N=80 rollouts per policy on a single task ('close drawer'), which is a small-scale and subjective downstream validation; no automated verifier or additional tasks are provided.

The 'first to systematically explore this problem' claim is somewhat overstated given concurrent and prior work on action-conditioned video diffusion world models (e.g., He et al. [24], IRASIM, AVID), which the paper acknowledges but distinguishes only on interactivity grounds.
Only one base model (DynamiCrafter) is tested; generality of the causalization recipe across architectures (e.g., DiT-based models) is unverified, which weakens the 'general approach' claim.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem: converting pre-trained video diffusion models into interactive, action-conditioned world models, and positions the two key challenges (causal generation and action conditioning) clearly.

The proposed pipeline (mixed weight transfer for causal convolutions, causal attention masking, Diffusion Forcing-style independent noise levels, and action dropout enabling classifier-free action guidance) is coherent and well-motivated, with clear pseudocode for training and sampling.

Experiments span two distinct domains (real-world robot manipulation on RT-1 and game simulation on CS:GO) and include a downstream application (Real2Sim policy evaluation), which goes beyond pure video-prediction metrics.

Quantitative results are strong: large improvements over DIAMOND on CS:GO (e.g., FVD 102.6 vs. 562.2) and competitive/superior results against transfer baselines on RT-1, plus ablations of both major components.

Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameter tables, implementation and metric descriptions in the appendix, and honest reporting of failure cases and of a bug in the baseline's FID computation.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core components are largely assembled from existing techniques—Diffusion Forcing [8] for independent noise levels, standard causal masking for attention, classifier-free guidance with conditioning dropout, and a simple kernel-initialization heuristic (mixed weight transfer). The framing as the 'first' systematic exploration overstates the delta over Diffusion Forcing and AVID [43], and Diffusion Forcing itself is not compared as a baseline (e.g., training the same backbone with Diffusion Forcing from scratch or with naive transfer).

Baseline comparisons raise fairness concerns. On CS:GO, the comparison against DIAMOND pits a 1.1B-parameter model pre-trained on internet-scale video against a model trained from scratch, at reduced resolution (outputs downsampled to 150×280), without controlling for compute or parameter count; the reported gains partly reflect the foundation-model prior rather than the proposed method.

The RT-1 results contain an unexplained anomaly: Vid2World/Vid2World-NAR have markedly worse FID (5.9) than all baselines (2.9–6.0, with the pre-trained base at 5.4) and even worse than the un-tuned base model on NAR FID, yet the text claims 'outperforms all prior methods by a significant margin' based mainly on FVD. This inconsistency is not discussed or analyzed.

Claims of enabling 'neural game engines' and interactive settings are not supported by any efficiency or latency analysis: inference uses 50 DDIM steps per frame plus an extra unconditional pass for guidance, which is likely far from real-time; no throughput measurements or speed comparisons with DIAMOND-Fast are provided despite interactivity being a central motivation.

The Real2Sim policy evaluation is thin: a single task ('close drawer'), N=80 rollouts per policy, and a subjective human verifier, with no quantification of verifier agreement, confidence intervals, or comparison to alternative evaluation protocols; conclusions about downstream decision-making utility rest on weak statistical ground.

Ablations are limited to one dataset (RT-1) with a reduced 30k-step budget, and no ablation of key hyperparameters (action dropout rate p, guidance scale λ, k_small) that the authors themselves acknowledge are important; the interaction between action guidance and rollout stability is not analyzed.

Writing quality is below the bar for a top-tier venue: multiple grammatical errors and typos ('principledly', 'perserves', 'dropping out', 'it's strong capabilities'), some figure/notation inconsistencies (e.g., Algorithm 3 line 7 conditioning term), and overclaiming language throughout the abstract and introduction.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: the paper cleanly decomposes the transformation of pre-trained video diffusion models into interactive world models into two barriers (causal generation and action conditioning), which makes the method easy to follow.

Practical and well-motivated techniques: causal masking for temporal attention is parameter-free, and the proposed mixed weight transfer for causal convolutions is a sensible, empirically validated alternative to naive shift-based weight transfer; the action-dropout scheme extends classifier-free guidance to frame-level actions in autoregressive settings in a principled way.

Strong and diverse evaluation: experiments span real-world robot manipulation (RT-1) and game simulation (CS:GO), with standard metrics (FVD, FID, SSIM, LPIPS, PSNR), a same-base-model comparison against multiple transfer baselines, and a valuable downstream application (Real2Sim policy evaluation) that goes beyond perceptual metrics.

Large quantitative gains on CS:GO versus DIAMOND (e.g., ~82% relative FVD improvement), and the best performance among transfer baselines on RT-1 in the non-autoregressive setting, where autoregressive baselines are not even applicable.

Good transparency: includes ablations of both key components (MWT and action guidance), training/sampling pseudocode, detailed hyperparameter tables, and candid discussion of failure cases and limitations.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: full inference details (guidance scale, rescale, k_small, sliding window), dataset splits, and training compute are documented.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty relative to prior work: the core training formulation is essentially Diffusion Forcing [8]; the main methodological additions are a fairly simple convolution weight-initialization scheme and action dropout for CFG. The claim of being the 'first' to systematically explore transferring pre-trained video diffusion models into interactive world models is overstated given AVID [43], He et al. [24], and interactive models like Oasis/Mineworld.

Baseline fairness concerns on CS:GO: DIAMOND is a much smaller model trained from scratch on domain data, while Vid2World starts from a 1.1B-parameter model pre-trained on internet-scale video. The large gains may largely reflect the pre-trained base model rather than the proposed transformation; there is no from-scratch or weaker-pretraining control to disentangle this.

Anomalous FID results in Table 1 are not adequately explained: Vid2World and Vid2World-NAR have FID (5.9-6.0) far worse than ControlNet/action-conditioned fine-tuning (2.9-3.2) despite winning other metrics; the footnote about AVID's code bug only covers baseline FIDs, leaving the paper's own FID behavior unexplained.
AVID itself, the most directly related transfer method, does not appear as an explicit row in Table 1; it is unclear whether a head-to-head comparison was performed.

Action controllability (the key claim of causal action guidance) is mostly evaluated qualitatively (Figures 9, 11); there is no quantitative action-alignment or counterfactual-controllability metric, and no comparison of guidance scales.

Long-horizon behavior is under-evaluated: metrics use only 16-frame rollouts; the 40-step Real2Sim evaluation covers a single task with human verification (N=80), which is thin evidence for downstream decision-making utility.

Inference cost is not addressed: 50 DDIM steps per frame in autoregressive rollout makes real-time interactivity (the 'neural game engine' motivation) questionable; no latency/throughput comparison against DIAMOND-Fast.
Ablations are run at only 30k steps due to compute limits, and hyperparameters (guidance scale 2.5, rescale 0.7) are hand-set per domain, which weakens the generality claims.

Mixed weight transfer lacks any analysis or justification beyond the empirical ablation (e.g., why averaging temporal weights is a good initialization); the writing also contains recurring typos ('casualization', 'principledly', 'it's performance') that detract from polish.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper decomposes the gap between pre-trained video diffusion models and interactive world models into two concrete challenges (causal generation and action conditioning), and addresses each with a targeted mechanism.

Novel and technically substantive component: the Extrapolative Weight Transfer scheme for causalizing temporal convolution layers is a genuinely new contribution, supported by a counter-example showing failure of naive shift transfer and a formal error bound (Proposition 1) in the appendix.

Comprehensive evaluation across three distinct domains (real-robot manipulation on RT-1, 3D game simulation on CS:GO, open-world navigation on RECON) with appropriate baselines built on the same base model (AVID, ControlNet, action/language-conditioned fine-tuning, DIAMOND, NWM), and strong reported results, including a large FVD/FID margin over DIAMOND on CS:GO.
Useful ablation study isolating the contributions of weight transfer mechanism and action guidance, with both components shown to matter.

Beyond video prediction metrics, the paper demonstrates downstream utility via Real2Sim policy evaluation, showing the world model can discriminate policy quality — a meaningful test of interactive world modeling rather than just video fidelity.

Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameter tables, training/inference pseudocode, dataset splits, evaluation protocol details, failure case analysis, and disclosure of a baseline metric computation issue (FID without eval mode) with corrected gray-italic reporting.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on existing techniques as building blocks: Diffusion Forcing (Chen et al., 2024) for noise-level heterogeneity and classifier-free guidance for action conditioning are adopted nearly as-is; the main novelty is the causalization/weight transfer and their combination, which some reviewers may view as incremental.

The 'interactive' claim is weakened by inference cost: 50 DDIM steps per frame with classifier-free guidance implies very low generation FPS, and no wall-clock/latency or throughput comparison against DIAMOND is reported — critical for a method pitched as a neural game engine / interactive world model.

Comparisons are not always fully apples-to-apples: on RECON, Vid2World is compared against NWM (a 1B DiT trained on large cross-domain action data) where training data scale and compute differ substantially, and single-step vs. auto-regressive setups introduce confounds the authors partially acknowledge.
Rollout horizon is short (16 frames; 20-frame context), and long-horizon stability/quality degradation of the causalized model is only qualitatively discussed; no quantitative long-rollout study.
Real2Sim policy evaluation relies on a small sample (N=50 trajectories, one task) and human verification as the success oracle, limiting statistical strength of that application claim.

Optimal guidance scale and other hyperparameters appear domain-dependent (authors note per-domain tuning may help), raising questions about robustness and tuning cost when transferring to new domains.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: converting pre-trained, non-causal video diffusion models into autoregressive, action-conditioned interactive world models, avoiding the prohibitive cost of training world models from scratch or collecting massive action-labeled data.

The framing of the two key challenges (causal generation and action conditioning) is clear, and the technical treatment is thorough: three systematically explored weight-transfer strategies for causalizing temporal convolutions, with a counter-example showing why naive shift transfer fails and an error bound (Proposition 1) justifying Extrapolative Weight Transfer.

Evaluation is unusually broad: three diverse domains (real-robot manipulation on RT-1, 3D game simulation on CS:GO, open-world navigation on RECON) with appropriate baselines that share the same base model where possible, plus a downstream application (Real2Sim policy evaluation) demonstrating utility beyond video metrics.

Strong quantitative results: Vid2World outperforms DIAMOND by large margins on CS:GO and matches or exceeds NWM on RECON despite harder autoregressive rollout settings; ablations isolate the contributions of weight transfer choice and action guidance.

The paper is transparent about limitations (failure cases in Appendix D, grayed-out FID numbers for AVID due to an evaluation-mode bug found in the released baseline code), and provides extensive implementation details, pseudocode, and hyperparameter tables supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely compositional rather than fundamental: causal masking of temporal attention, per-frame noise-level training (Diffusion Forcing, Chen et al. 2024), and classifier-free guidance with action dropout are all established techniques; the most original element (Extrapolative Weight Transfer) is a fairly local weight-reassignment trick restricted to kernel size 3, and the ablation shows Masked Weight Transfer is nearly as effective.

The claim of building an 'interactive' world model is undercut by inference cost: 50-step DDIM sampling per frame means autoregressive rollout is far from real-time, yet no inference latency/throughput comparison is reported, which is critical for the interactive game-simulation and decision-making use cases the paper motivates.

Baselines across domains are not fully commensurate: on RECON, comparisons against NWM involve a 1B model trained on different data with different prediction regimes (single-step vs. autoregressive, different fps), and PSNR/SSIM-style pixel metrics are of questionable value for stochastic world modeling where multiple valid futures exist.

Rollout horizons are short (16-20 frames); error accumulation over long horizons—the central failure mode for autoregressive world models—is only briefly probed, and the Real2Sim evaluation relies on human verification of only 50 trajectories on a single task (close drawer).
Ablations are conducted at 30k training steps for computational reasons, so the reported component rankings may not hold at the full 100k-step training budget used for the main results.

Theoretical analysis assumes L-smooth (twice-differentiable) underlying feature sequences, an assumption that is difficult to verify for deep-network activations and whose practical relevance to the observed ablation gaps is not clearly established.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper identifies two concrete barriers (causal generation and action conditioning) to repurposing pre-trained video diffusion models as interactive world models, and addresses both systematically.

The proposed Extrapolative Weight Transfer is a genuinely novel and principled technical contribution, supported by a counter-example showing failure of naive shift transfer and a full error-bound derivation in Appendix A, which is rare rigor for this line of work.

Causal Action Guidance is a clean, well-designed extension of classifier-free guidance with frame-level action dropout that enables test-time steering of interactivity — a useful capability beyond plain action-conditioned fine-tuning.

Extensive evaluation across three diverse domains (real robot manipulation RT-1, 3D game simulation CS:GO, open-world navigation RECON) with strong quantitative gains over appropriate and competitive baselines (AVID, ControlNet, DIAMOND, NWM) built on comparable data/base models.
Thoughtful downstream demonstration (Real2Sim policy evaluation) showing the world model is actually useful for decision-making, not just video prediction metrics.

Honest and informative ablations (weight transfer mechanisms x action guidance), explicit documentation of evaluation-metric discrepancies found in prior work (AVID FID computation), and candid failure-case analysis in the appendix.
Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameter tables, algorithms for training/sampling/evaluation, and clear implementation details.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental in parts: the training objective directly adopts Diffusion Forcing (Chen et al., 2024), causal masking of temporal attention is a standard operation, and action guidance is a straightforward adaptation of classifier-free guidance; the strongest novel element is the weight transfer scheme.

Comparisons in the navigation domain are not perfectly apples-to-apples: NWM is a 1B model trained on cross-domain action-labeled data and evaluated in a single-step setting, while Vid2World uses harder autoregressive rollout — favorable framing, but resolution/context-length differences complicate interpretation.
Computational cost remains high (100k steps, ~6-7 days on 4x A100 per domain), and the paper acknowledges this without a strong solution; scaling behavior beyond a 1.4B U-Net base model is untested.
Key inference hyperparameters (guidance scale 2.5, guidance rescale 0.7, k_small) appear hand-picked and are admitted to be under-tuned; sensitivity analysis of these choices is missing.
Ablation studies are conducted at only 30k gradient steps (vs 100k for main results), so conclusions about component contributions may not fully transfer to the final models.

Evaluation relies heavily on perceptual metrics (FVD/FID/LPIPS/DreamSim); the only action-faithfulness evidence is qualitative (counterfactual rollout figures) plus a small human-verified Real2Sim study (N=50, one task), so quantitative action-controllability measurement is thin.
No code or model release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of the transfer recipe despite detailed documentation.
